paras: The lynching of Joe Barnes, Vance Brandt and Julia Brandt was the hanging of three young Black people by a crowd near Salem, Clarendon County, South Carolina, on December 8, 1880. Accused of killing Ada Kennedy, a young white woman, at her home three days earlier, they were hanged near the spot after the crowd voted against holding them for court. Wire reports carried it nationally, and South Carolina papers defended it in editorials.

According to a letter to the News and Courier from New Zion, Ada Kennedy, 19 or 20 and formerly Ada Wright of Darlington, was found dead outside her front gate near Salem on Sunday, December 5, about three hours after her husband Thomas left to fetch his mother. An inquest returned a verdict of "murder in the highest degree by unknown hands," and wire versions added that she was expecting twins.

After others were arrested and released, Joe Barnes, about 16, who had worked for Kennedy the week before, was arrested on Tuesday, four miles from the scene, and confessed under questioning. In his confession as printed, Vance Brandt, 18, and his sister Julia, 15, had Barnes signal when Kennedy left so they could rob the house; Vance struck her down and Julia cut her with a hoe. The Brandts denied any part, saying the blood on their clothes came from a chicken and partridges, but the correspondent cited bloody clothing, Kennedy's money and pistol, and finger marks on a hoe handle said to match Julia's shawl.

The Kingstree correspondent counted about 150 white men and 50 Black men and women in the crowd; the New Zion letter put it at 250 to 300 citizens "both white and colored." Both the Kingstree dispatch and the December 11 wire reported that Black people present asked to burn the prisoners alive, that the whites refused, and that a vote was taken on jailing or lynching them. Only 23 voted to await the law, by the Kingstree count.

At 4 p.m. on Wednesday, halters from nearby stables were fastened to the nearest tree, within twenty yards of the place of the killing, according to the Kingstree dispatch. The three were made to mount a cart beneath the limb; Barnes asked to pray, Vance said only "Lord have mercy," and with handkerchiefs over their faces the cart was pushed away.
No report of an inquest on the three, or of any arrest or official inquiry into the lynching, appears in the coverage, and the Kingstree dispatch noted that no clue implicated anyone else.

The first report, a Charleston dispatch of December 9 on "three negroes, one woman and two men, who murdered Mrs. Kennedy," ran on December 10 in New York, Chicago, Richmond and Portland papers. Headlines presented it as deserved punishment: the Savannah Morning News titled it "Speedy Justice," and the Richmond Dispatch's summary spoke of "three negro murderers summarily punished by 'Judge Lynch.'" The fuller December 11 dispatch, built on Barnes's reported confession, followed in papers from St. Paul and Dallas to Columbus and Savannah, under heads such as "A Bad Batch" in Chicago.

South Carolina papers reprinted the New Zion letter under headlines such as "Vengeance, Swift and Sure" in the Winnsboro News and Herald and "The Clarendon Outrage and Its Speedy Punishment" in the Abbeville Press and Banner. The Abbeville paper's editorial argued that murderers so seldom suffered in South Carolina courts that "these facts have almost created a necessity for lynch law." The Orangeburg Democrat called the three "young colored demons" and, while saying it was no advocate of extreme measures, judged this a case in which it became "proper and necessary to deal summarily with offenders."

Criticism arrived secondhand: the Hartwell Sun in Georgia quoted the New York Herald deprecating "such frequent resort to these mob executions" and replied that the North, East and West resorted to lynch law as often.

The New Zion letter dated the killing Sunday, December 5, and the Orangeburg Democrat the 4th; the hanging is dated Wednesday, December 8, by the two earliest dispatches. Ages varied: the Wilmington Daily Gazette gave 20, 16 and 12, the Dallas Daily Herald gave Vance as 13, and the Orangeburg paper gave 15, 16 and 18.

framing.detail: South Carolina heads 'Vengeance, Swift and Sure' and 'The Guilt Fully Proved'.
Abbeville editorial: court failures 'have almost created a necessity for lynch law'.

Savannah 'Speedy Justice'; Richmond 'summarily punished by "Judge Lynch"'.
Northern and Western dailies ran the Dec. 9 brief and the Dec. 11 narrative without comment.
Hartwell Sun reprinted the New York Herald's deprecation of 'mob executions' and rebutted it.

acts.note: Barnes arrested Tuesday four miles from the scene; victim arrest.
Vance and Julia Brandt also held on suspicion (bloody clothes); date and holders not stated.
Black men and women present begged to be allowed to take the prisoners and burn them alive; whites refused.
Crowd debated and voted whether to jail the three or lynch them; only 23 voted to await the law.
Prisoners taken by the crowd; who held them beforehand is not stated.
Halters fastened to a limb, three made to mount a cart, cart pushed away about 4 p.m.; all three hanged.
